To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) polyphagous whiteflies harbor transient bacterial communities in their gut that change during adaptation to a new host, (ii) these transient communities can be enriched in degradative capabilities that might facilitate the adaptation of the insect to a new host and (iii) the enrichment of these capabilities in the transient community is correlated with an increase in the survival of the insects on the new host, suggesting a role in the adaptation process.

the adaptation process of whiteflies to a novel host plant is associated with changes in the composition of their gut microbiota, with a predicted increase in the metabolic pathways of secondary metabolite degradation, and with an increase in the insect survival on the new host plant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the microbiome in the host plant adaptation process of the polyphagous whitefly, Bemisia tabaco.
the role of microbiota in insect adaptation to new hosts, a phenomenon that may be important in the context of global climate change.

the dynamics of the microbiota of the whitefly during host plant adaptation, which is of importance for the understanding of host plant adaptation in general and for developing pest control strategies in particular.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the gut microbiota can be a major factor in host adaptation of polyphagous herbivores.
gut-associated microbes are an additional flexible metabolic tool-box to polyphagous insects to facilitate a quick host switching.
the adaptation process to a new plant host by a generalist sap feeding insect may be partially facilitated by the presence of a transient gut-associated bacterial community.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
“the microbiota can make the difference between life and death”.
“The gut microbiota can provide generalist herbivores with an additional “tool-box” for overcoming plant defenses”.
the gut microbiota of polyphagous insects is not a static entity and can play an active role in the host’s adaptation to new host plants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the insect’s gut microbiota can be a key factor in the adaptation to novel host plants.
the gut-associated bacterial communities are dynamic and that their composition and diversity can change rapidly in response to host plant changes.
insects can rely on transient associations for overcoming the host-plant adaptation process.
